reading.body:
Retail AI is tracked by four independent sources covering adoption, store technology, market size, and software spend, but none of them measures the compute or power behind those systems.

The four sources form a layered measurement stack. Census BTOS updates adoption every two weeks across all sectors, including retail trade. NRF adds detail on store automation, inventory computer vision, and customer-experience software. Coresight sizes the market for merchandising and supply-chain logistics, while IHL tracks software expenditure and operational return in grocery, apparel, and general merchandise. Adoption is measured rather than guessed, and the Census series updates often enough to show change.

For AI specifically, the volume use cases are demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation. These run across many stores and transactions, so even small changes in adoption or software spend can signal where inference workloads are growing. But the data stops at adoption and spend. None of the four sources reports electricity demand, data center capacity, or compute requirements, so the data cannot support claims about grid constraints or building needs for retail AI.

summary: Demand forecasting, recommendation, and customer-service automation are the volume use cases.

analysis.body:
The Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey measures AI use in retail trade, NAICS 44-45, by asking firms whether they used AI in the last two weeks. The latest reading is 16.5%, against a prior period of 15.5%. The series was first asked in September 2023 and is updated fortnightly, which makes it the closest thing this sector has to a running adoption count rather than a one-off survey estimate.

What that adoption consists of is described across the trade sources. The National Retail Federation covers store automation, inventory computer vision and customer-experience software, and its account of conversations in Paris centered on practical AI, connected stores and relationship-driven loyalty. Coresight Research produces adoption rates and market sizing for AI in merchandising and supply-chain logistics. The deployments this page covers are demand forecasting, recommendation and customer-service automation at volume. A concrete example from the IHL Group's page is Crocs, which replaced scripted self-service with Rivet, a Salesforce Agentforce-powered conversational assistant unifying product discovery, customer support and order tracking, with plans to extend it to HEYDUDE and multilingual international markets.

Money and vendors concentrate in a few visible places. IHL Group tracks retail technology expenditure and operational return across grocery, apparel and general merchandise, and reports that most retail AI budgets fund the wrong layer first, with pilots stalling before they reach the store floor. Albertsons Media Collective launched incrementality-based multi-touch attribution with LiveRamp, linking exposure data across owned channels, Meta, offsite media and third-party inventory to Albertsons transaction data, and expanded Criteo-powered AI search and YouTube branded-content advertising. Amazon Web Services launched Amazon Connect Talent, an agentic hiring platform that automates high-volume recruiting, creates interview plans, schedules and conducts 24/7 voice interviews, and gives recruiters transcripts, notes and scoring.

Demand on the shopper side is measured by Acosta Group, whose findings appear in the IHL material: 34% of shoppers use AI tools for shopping, led by ChatGPT and Google Gemini, and 25% routinely use Gemini for product searches. Gen Z and millennials drive that adoption, using AI for comparisons, research and in-store decisions, though only 22% trust agents to purchase autonomously. That last figure is the clearest signal in the sources about how far autonomy currently extends on the consumer side.

The strongest return evidence is operational rather than financial. IHL Group's 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, in cooperation with Chain Store Age, finds that inventory data accuracy, not AI budget size, separates specialty retail winners from laggards. IHL also reports inventory distortion down to $1.7 trillion, with empty shelves still costing $690.9 billion. Crocs' stated expectations, improved autonomous resolution, search success, click-through rates and basket size, are expectations rather than measured outcomes in the material available.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the sources point in one direction: the constraint is data quality and where the budget lands, not the size of the AI line item. The cited material does not address regulation or compliance posture for retail AI, so nothing here should be read as guidance on that front.

https://nrf.com/.brief: The National Retail Federation describes itself as an advocate for the people, policies, and ideas that support a thriving retail sector, and it provides retail news, insights, and industry events. According to the organization, conversations held in Paris illustrated how retailers are putting what it calls "The Next Now" into practice. These efforts span practical artificial intelligence, connected stores, and loyalty programs built on relationships.

https://coresight.com/.brief: Coresight Research describes itself as a provider of data-based analysis focused on retail and technology, and says it has unique expertise in China within the industry. The page also states that the firm runs an exclusive, invite-only collaborative forum that examines AI opportunities and challenges for consumer-focused businesses. No market data or research findings are presented on this page.

https://ihlservices.com/.brief: IHL Group conducts research on retail technology spending and strategy. According to their 2026 study of 96 specialty retail brands, inventory data accuracy rather than AI budget size determines which specialty retailers succeed, and most retail AI budgets fund the wrong infrastructure layer first. The organisation also reports that inventory distortion has declined to $1.7 trillion, though empty shelves still cost $690.9 billion annually. IHL's analysis finds that the presence of AI does not predict pricing-platform quality among vendors, and retailers should instead evaluate explainability, automation controls, and governance safeguards.
